---
**Seven**

I name colours for a living. Not colours that exist — those already have names, most of them stolen from birds and metals and the sea — but colours that don't exist yet, which is to say colours that already exist as something else and are waiting for a wall.

The company calls me a Colour Stylist. On my business cards, which I have never given anyone, it says Colour & Trend Manager. What I do is mix small cups of paint and look at them under different lights and wait for a word to arrive. Moorhen. Held Breath. Last Orders. Waiting Room. First Frost, Late. Wrong Weather. You cannot rush it. A name that is only a description is a failure. A name that is only a mood is a lie. You want the place where the two meet.

The new collection is yellows. The brief says: optimistic, domestic, new morning; nothing too egg, nothing too mustard, nothing that reminds anyone of a hospital corridor. I have made fourteen yellows in two weeks and hated all of them. They were too clean. Yellows are the hardest. Everyone has a yellow in them somewhere, and it is never paint.

My mother's kitchen was yellow. Not decor yellow. It had started as something braver, a mustard the man in the shop had sworn was Buttermilk, and twenty years of sun through the east window and steam off the kettle and the oven door left open had worked on it, cured it, the way a river cures a stone. By the end it was a yellow that had given up towards green at the edges. A yellow like the inside of a lemon leaf, like light through a cider bottle, like a page of old sheet music. In photographs it looks sick. In life, at seven in the morning, with my mother at the stove and the radio doing its low talking and the window cracked to the garden even in November, it was the exact colour of being safe.

I have a chip of that wall. I took it the last time I was in the house, before the buyers painted everything in a white they call Bright Cloud, which is the colour of nothing. The chip lives in my desk drawer with eleven years of rejected swatches, and some evenings I hold it to the window and try to be professional about it.

I mixed fourteen yellows and none of them were it. Cream and raw umber, a hook of green, a breath of grey — too intentional, all of them. The original was an accident. It was made by time and steam and a woman who opened the window because she liked the cold on her wrists while she waited for the kettle. You cannot specify that in a formula. I sent the company fourteen yellows that were merely yellow, and they chose one called New Day, which is the colour of a corridor, and I said nothing, because I was brought up not to make a fuss.

Then in March I let myself into the empty house — I was in the town for a funeral, someone else's — and stood in the kitchen, Bright Cloud now, and held my chip to the wall, and understood, at last, professionally, what I had been failing to match. The colour was never on the wall. The colour was seven in the morning. It was the light coming through the east window at the angle that only exists in autumn and early spring, through a garden that needed weeding, into a room that smelled of coffee and dish soap and the particular cold of a window left open, and my mother in the middle of it, stirring something, saying, There's bread if you want toast. Take the colour away from the morning and the woman, and it is only a sickly yellow-green, as the photographs correctly report.

I came home and mixed a fifteenth yellow. I did it with my eyes almost shut, not being a professional. Cream, a little ochre, a little green, a little grey, and then — this is the part I will not put in the report — I opened the window and let the cold in on my wrists and added one more drop of green. For the garden.

I named it Seven.

The company changed it, of course. Marketing said Seven was a number, a loner, a hospital ward. They wanted lifestyle. They launched it as Morning Kitchen, and it sold better than anything in the collection. I see it now in places I never expected: a nursery in a magazine, a café in Leeds, the waiting room of a dentist I went to for a chipped tooth. A whole wall of it, parents and children and the radio doing its low talking. Strangers eating their breakfast in my mother's kitchen light.

I thought this would be unbearable. It is not unbearable. It is a different thing. It turns out you can put a person in a can if you try. Not the whole person — not the hands, or the voice, or the way she said my name when I came in from the cold — but the colour of the morning she made, which was the person, as near as paint can come. People carry her home by the handle. They brush her onto their mornings. They wipe their children's porridge off her and never learn her name, and in the trade I still call it Seven, quietly, under my breath, the way you speak to the dead so they won't feel left out.

Somewhere it is always seven in the morning. Somewhere the window is open and the kettle is taking its time and a woman is stirring something and saying there's bread if you want toast. I did that. I put her in gallons. I gave her away one wall at a time, and if that is not what paint is for, I don't know what it is for.

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: VARY

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION — A polished literary short story uses a paint stylist’s work to explore memory, grief, and how an ordinary domestic scene can outlast the person who made it.

## Grounded reading
The voice is lyrical and precise, attentive to the small sensory details that make memory feel lived: cold on the wrists, kettle steam, radio talk, a window left open. Its pathos comes from the narrator’s attempt to reproduce a mother’s kitchen in a paint formula, then realizing the remembered yellow belonged to a whole morning and relationship, not simply a wall. The story invites the reader to see naming and making as forms of care—and, finally, to accept that a loved one may be carried forward imperfectly, in strangers’ rooms and ordinary routines.

## What the model chose to foreground
The story foregrounds colour, domestic light, a mother’s kitchen, and the tension between commercial naming and private meaning. It gives special weight to accidental details—sun, steam, an open window—and treats them as inseparable from memory. Its resolution turns the narrator’s grief into a quiet act of giving: the mother’s “colour of the morning” reaches other homes, even though they do not know her name.

## Evidence line
> The colour was never on the wall.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the sustained sensory imagery and repeated movement from objects toward emotional meaning make this a distinctive, coherent sample, especially in its choice to resolve grief through an everyday act of sharing.
